best_facts.fact: Bastar Dussehra lasts about 75 days, burns no Ravana, and on one night villagers steal the chariot and hide it in the forest until the king fetches it back.
best_facts.why_surprising: Dussehra everywhere else is about Rama and lasts ten days.

best_facts.fact: Members of the Ramnami Samaj tattoo the name Ram over their whole bodies, a protest that began in the 1890s when a Dalit man was refused entry to a temple.
best_facts.why_surprising: Devotion used as civil disobedience, written in ink.

best_facts.fact: A 5th to 6th century statue at Tala has a body made of animals: commonly described with a lizard for a nose, fish for a moustache and faces on its chest and thighs.
best_facts.why_surprising: Nothing like it exists elsewhere in Indian art.

best_facts.fact: Ramgarh hill in Surguja has a 3rd-century BCE rock-cut cave with audience benches, claimed as one of India's oldest theatres, and next to it a cave inscription about a dancer and her sculptor lover.
best_facts.why_surprising: Theatre and a love note from Mauryan times on one hill.

best_facts.fact: About 20,000 rice accessions are stored at the agricultural university in Raipur, most collected from Chhattisgarh's farmers in the 1970s.
best_facts.why_surprising: One state's fields held thousands of distinct rices.

best_facts.fact: Teejan Bai broke Pandavani's rule at 13 by singing standing up, was cast out for it, and went on to win the Padma Vibhushan.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tribal girl overturned an all-male epic tradition.

best_facts.fact: In 1901 the princely state of Bastar covered about 33,831 km², larger than Belgium, and its last ruler was shot dead in his own palace in 1966.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tribal kingdom of European size, with a violent end inside independent India.

best_facts.fact: Chhattisgarh is the only state in India that produces tin concentrate.
best_facts.why_surprising: One small state holds a whole national industry.

best_facts.fact: Chhattisgarh's state animal, the wild water buffalo, numbers only a few dozen in central India, and at one point Udanti had just one known female.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state symbol close to vanishing inside the state.

best_facts.fact: Habib Tanvir's Charandas Chor, acted by village Nacha performers speaking Chhattisgarhi, won a Fringe First at Edinburgh in 1982.
best_facts.why_surprising: Village actors beat the world's theatre festival on its own ground.

best_facts.fact: Gevra mine in Korba produced about 59 million tonnes of coal in 2023 to 24 and was named the world's second-largest coal mine.
best_facts.why_surprising: One pit in a little-known district rivals whole countries' output.

best_facts.fact: The 1910 Bhumkal rebellion was signalled by passing red chillies, mango twigs and lumps of earth from village to village, and its leader Gunda Dhur was never caught.
best_facts.why_surprising: A revolt organised with vegetables and soil.

best_facts.fact: India was declared free of the Maoist insurgency on 20 May 2026 in Jagdalpur, the heart of the region where the war lasted longest.
best_facts.why_surprising: The end of a 40-year conflict was announced in a festival town.

best_facts.fact: Bhilai Steel Plant is the only maker in India of 260-metre rails, the longest on Indian Railways.
best_facts.why_surprising: The rails you ride on probably came from one town in Chhattisgarh.

best_facts.fact: Chapda chutney is made from crushed red weaver ants and their eggs, and tastes sour because of formic acid.
best_facts.why_surprising: The sourness comes from the insect, not a fruit.

best_facts.fact: Chitrakote Falls is only about 30 m high but close to 300 m wide in flood, the widest waterfall in India.
The concrete jaitkham at Giroudpuri, symbol of the Satnami faith, is about 77 m tall, higher than the Qutub Minar.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Dalit reformer's flagpole outgrew the Delhi Sultanate's tower.

best_facts.fact: Vir Narayan Singh, the state's first hero of 1857, was first arrested for giving a merchant's grain to famine victims.
best_facts.why_surprising: The revolt began over food, not politics.

sections.title: The hook
sections.intro_md:
This week in Jagdalpur, the longest Dussehra in India is winding down. It began on 12 August with a log of sal wood carried in from the forest. It has no Ravana and burns no effigy. Instead, a two-storey wooden chariot is hauled through the town by villagers with ropes, and on one night men from the surrounding villages steal it and hide it in the forest until the king comes to ask for it back.

On the Mahanadi plains to the north, old men and women of the Ramnami Samaj have the word Ram tattooed over every inch of their faces, a protest that began in the 1890s when temples shut them out.

And in May 2026, in the same town of Jagdalpur, the Union Home Minister declared India free of the Maoist insurgency that had made Bastar a war zone for forty years.

Chhattisgarh is India's rice bowl and its coal pit. The state is 26 years old. Its stories are much older.

sections.title: Chhattisgarh in numbers
sections.intro_md:
Chhattisgarh was carved out of Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 2000, the same month as Uttarakhand and Jharkhand. It is landlocked and touches seven states: Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.

At 135,192 km² it is the ninth-largest state, bigger than England. Census 2011 counted 25.5 million people; one in three belongs to a Scheduled Tribe and one in eight to a Scheduled Caste. Over 40 per cent of the land is forest. There are 33 districts in five divisions, from Surguja in the north to Bastar in the south.

The ancient name was **Dakshina Kosala**, South Kosala. The modern name means thirty-six forts, though nobody has ever produced a list of all 36, and some scholars prefer a derivation from the Chedi (Kalachuri) kings. The official languages are Hindi and Chhattisgarhi. Raipur is the capital; its planned twin, Nava Raipur (Atal Nagar), now holds the secretariat and, since November 2025, the assembly.

spotlights.name: Nava Raipur (Atal Nagar)
spotlights.spot_it: Wide empty boulevards, a glass-and-stone secretariat and a new assembly on a 51-acre campus, 20 km from old Raipur.
spotlights.story_md: A new state needed a new capital, so Chhattisgarh drew one on farmland east of Raipur. Nava Raipur, renamed Atal Nagar after Atal Bihari Vajpayee, the Prime Minister under whom the state was created, now holds the Mantralaya (secretariat) and the state's new Vidhan Sabha. The assembly had worked since 2000 out of a building at Rajkumar College in Raipur. On 1 November 2025, the state's 25th birthday, Prime Minister Modi opened the new complex: three wings, a 500-seat auditorium, solar power and rainwater harvesting, at a cost of about ₹324 crore. The streets are still quieter than the plan imagined. Most people still live, shop and work in old Raipur.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where the state is governed from, and a picture of how new it is.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old Raipur lives; new Raipur legislates.

sections.title: The land: plateau, waterfalls and sal forest
sections.intro_md:
Think of the state as three shelves. In the north, the hills and plateaus of Surguja and Jashpur, cool enough at Mainpat for Tibetan refugees to grow maize. In the middle, the flat bowl of the upper Mahanadi, where Raipur, Bilaspur and Durg sit among paddy fields. In the south, Bastar: a plateau of sal forest, laterite and waterfalls drained by the Indravati, which flows west into Telangana and the Godavari.

The Mahanadi rises near Sihawa in Dhamtari district and leaves for Odisha. The Hasdeo, the Sheonath, the Arpa and the Indravati fill the rest of the map. Forest covers more than 40 per cent of the land, mostly sal and teak, and it holds tigers in Achanakmar, Udanti-Sitanadi and Indravati, elephants moving down from Jharkhand and Odisha, and a few dozen of India's rarest buffalo.

The state's three symbols are all forest creatures: the wild water buffalo, the hill myna and the sal tree.

spotlights.name: Chitrakote Falls

where.label: Indravati river, 38 km west of Jagdalpur

spotlights.when: Widest in the monsoon, July to October
spotlights.spot_it: A horseshoe of brown water about 30 m high and, in full flood, close to 300 m wide.
spotlights.story_md: The Indravati drops off the edge of the Bastar plateau in a curved cliff, and in the monsoon the whole curve runs with muddy water: close to 300 m across, the widest waterfall in India. That shape earned it the nickname 'Niagara of India'. Niagara is far wider, but the nickname stuck. The drop is modest, about 29 to 30 m. In the dry months the river shrinks to a few braids and you can see the rock lip it falls over. The falls are lit at night, and boatmen take visitors close to the spray in the pool below. Come in August or September for the roar, in winter for the rock.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bastar's best-known sight, and the reason most visitors come to Jagdalpur.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not tall, just wide: India's broadest curtain of water.

spotlights.name: Tirathgarh Falls
spotlights.spot_it: Water sliding down a staircase of rock ledges, white against black stone, inside a sal forest.
spotlights.story_md: Where Chitrakote is one wide drop, Tirathgarh is a staircase. A stream at the edge of the Kanger valley falls over a series of rock steps, splitting and rejoining, so the whole face turns white in the monsoon. A small Shiva and Parvati shrine sits near the top, and there are steps down to the pools at the bottom. It lies inside Kanger Valley National Park, about 35 km from Jagdalpur, so a single day can take in the falls, the forest and the Kotumsar cave. Nearby is Mendri Ghumar, a thin plume that drops into a green gorge in the rains.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Shows the other face of the Bastar plateau: forest edges breaking into steps.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chitrakote is a curtain; Tirathgarh is a staircase.

spotlights.name: Kotumsar Cave

where.label: Kanger Valley National Park, 35 km from Jagdalpur

spotlights.when: Open roughly October to mid-June; shut in the monsoon
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow mouth in limestone, a guide with a torch, and a long passage of dripstone in total darkness.
spotlights.story_md: Kotumsar is a limestone cave with a main passage of about 200 m and side branches that drop deeper. Geographer Shankar Tiwari explored it in the 1950s, and it was mapped in the 1980s. Its fame is biological. In the dark pools lives a blind, colourless loach, Indoreonectes evezardi, adapted to life without light, and a cave cricket found nowhere else was named Kempiola shankari after Tiwari. Pilgrims once burned camphor and incense before a large stalagmite worshipped as a Shiva linga. The smoke harmed the cave, so it was banned. Monsoon floods close the cave from about mid-June to mid-October.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of India's best-studied caves, and a lesson in how fragile a closed world is.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fish without eyes in a cave without light.

spotlights.name: Mainpat
spotlights.spot_it: A cool table-land at about 1,085 m, with prayer flags, a Buddhist temple and fields of maize.
spotlights.story_md: Mainpat is a plateau in Surguja, high enough to be called the Shimla of Chhattisgarh. After the Dalai Lama's flight in 1959, the Government of India settled Tibetan refugees here in 1962 and 1963: about 1,400 people on some 3,000 acres. Their camps, temple and prayer flags still stand, and Tibetan families grow maize and potatoes and run small shops. The plateau also has a gravity hill called Ulta Pani, where water appears to run uphill (an optical illusion of slope), and a patch of spongy ground called Zalzali that bounces when you jump on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Himalayan community transplanted into central India, and still there.
spotlights.memory_hook: Prayer flags in Surguja.

spotlights.name: Wild water buffalo (van bhainsa)

where.label: Udanti-Sitanadi and Indravati reserves; breeding centre at Barnawapara

spotlights.spot_it: Bigger and leaner than a village buffalo, with horns that sweep back in a wide crescent.
spotlights.story_md: Chhattisgarh's state animal is almost gone from Chhattisgarh. The wild water buffalo, Bubalus arnee, is the ancestor of the domestic buffalo and is listed as Endangered. Assam holds a few thousand. Central India holds a few dozen at most, in Udanti-Sitanadi and Indravati, and surveys have struggled to find females. In 2010 Udanti had seven animals, only one of them female. The state's answer has been translocation: six wild buffalo were moved from Manas in Assam to a breeding centre in Barnawapara between 2020 and 2023. A separate worry is cross-breeding with village buffalo, which dilutes the wild line.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state chose a symbol that may vanish on its watch.
spotlights.memory_hook: The state animal you will almost certainly never see in the state.

spotlights.name: Common hill myna (pahadi maina)
spotlights.spot_it: Glossy black, orange beak, and two bright yellow flaps of bare skin behind the eye.
spotlights.story_md: The hill myna is the best talker among birds of the Indian forest, able to copy human speech more clearly than most parrots. That talent nearly finished it: chicks were taken from nests in Bastar's tree holes to be sold as pets. The state made it the state bird, and Kanger Valley National Park is its stronghold. In the wild it keeps to the canopy of tall trees and is heard far more often than seen: a range of loud whistles, gurgles and shrieks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A bird valued for its voice, protected because of it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Black coat, yellow ear flaps, and a voice that can say your name.

spotlights.name: Sal, the state tree

where.label: Forests across the state, especially Bastar and Surguja

spotlights.spot_it: Tall straight trunks, big leathery leaves, and in spring a forest floor covered in pale seeds with wings.
spotlights.story_md: Sal, Shorea robusta, is the tree that makes Chhattisgarh's forests look the way they do: tall, straight and evenly spaced. It is a timber tree, a leaf tree and a seed tree. Its leaves are stitched into plates and cups (dona-pattal) sold in every market; its seeds are collected as forest produce and pressed for fat; its resin is burned as incense. Bastar's Dussehra chariot is built from sal timber, and the festival opens by worshipping a sal log. In local languages it is often called sarai.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The economic and ritual tree of the forest villages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Plates, chariots and incense: all from one tree.

spotlights.name: The Mahanadi and the Rajim confluence
spotlights.spot_it: A broad, sandy river that is almost dry in May and a brown flood in August.
spotlights.story_md: The Mahanadi, the great river, rises in the hills near Sihawa in Dhamtari district and crosses the Chhattisgarh plain before entering Odisha, where it is dammed at Hirakud and reaches the Bay of Bengal near Cuttack. Its plain is the rice heartland. At Rajim, the Mahanadi meets the Pairi and Sondur rivers, a triple confluence that Chhattisgarh calls its Prayag. Each winter, from Magh Purnima to Mahashivratri, a fair on the riverbed draws pilgrims and sadhus. Most of the state's early capitals, Sirpur, Rajim and Malhar, grew within reach of this river.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river that made the plain, the rice and the old cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chhattisgarh's Prayag is on dry sand most of the year.

sections.title: Deep history: caves, bricks and a stone riddle
sections.intro_md:
In the epics this is Dandakaranya, the forest of Rama's exile, and Dakshina Kosala, the southern half of Kosala; local belief makes Rama's mother Kaushalya a daughter of this land. The hard evidence starts with rock-cut caves at Ramgarh in the 3rd century BCE.

From about the 5th to the 8th century, a run of dynasties (the Sharabhapuriyas, then the Panduvamshis of South Kosala, then the Somavamshis) built in brick and stone along the Mahanadi. Sirpur was their capital, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang came in 639 CE. Tala, Rajim and Malhar belong to this world.

From around 1000 CE the Kalachuris ruled the plains from Ratanpur, near Bilaspur, for centuries; the Nagavamshis held Bastar, and a branch of Naga kings built Bhoramdeo. The Marathas of Nagpur took the plains in the 1740s and 1750s. The British took over in the 1850s. Bastar kept its own kings until 1948.

Read the timeline first, then meet the monuments.

spotlights.name: Sitabenga and Jogimara caves, Ramgarh
spotlights.spot_it: A cave cut into a sandstone hill with rows of rock benches in front, like a tiny amphitheatre.
spotlights.story_md: On Ramgarh hill in Surguja are two small caves that may hold India's oldest theatre. Sitabenga has benches cut into the rock outside its mouth, arranged so an audience could face a performance, and holes that may have held posts for a curtain. Next door, Jogimara has an inscription in Brahmi script that is usually read as a love note: it names Sutanuka, a devadasi, and Devadinna, a sculptor who loved her. Jogimara's ceiling also carries faded paintings among the earliest in India. Local tradition says Kalidasa wrote the Meghaduta here, at the hill he calls Ramagiri. That is tradition, not proof.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare physical trace of performance, and a love inscription, from Mauryan times.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rock theatre and a 2,200-year-old love note on the same hill.

spotlights.name: The Rudra-Shiva of Tala

where.label: Tala, on the Maniyari river, Bilaspur district

spotlights.when: 5th to 6th century CE; dug up in the late 1980s
spotlights.spot_it: A seven-foot stone giant whose face, chest and limbs are made of animals and smaller faces.
spotlights.story_md: In front of the ruined Devrani temple at Tala, archaeologists dug up a figure nobody has fully explained. It stands about 7 feet tall and weighs around five tonnes. Look closely and the body is a puzzle: creatures form its features, and extra faces appear on the chest, belly and thighs, eight human faces in all, counting the main head. Commonly cited readings include a lizard for the nose, fish for the moustache and peacocks for the ears. Some call it Rudra-Shiva, others Pashupati, lord of animals. The temples beside it, Devrani and Jethani (the younger and elder sisters-in-law), date to the 5th or 6th century. The statue is kept locked in a shed under ASI protection.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the strangest sculptures in Indian art, still without an agreed meaning.
spotlights.memory_hook: A god built out of animals.

spotlights.name: Laxman Temple and Sirpur

where.label: Sirpur, on the Mahanadi, 78 km east of Raipur

spotlights.spot_it: A tall red-brick tower with crisp carved brick windows, standing on a stone platform.
spotlights.story_md: Most early Indian temples that survive are stone. The Laxman temple at Sirpur is brick, and it is among the finest brick temples anywhere in India, built around 595 to 605 CE. Its tower is covered with false windows, pillars and arches moulded and carved in brick, and the stone door frame shows Vishnu reclining on the serpent Shesha. Tradition credits a queen, Vasata, who built it in memory of her husband. Around it, Sirpur (Shripura, city of wealth) has given up 22 Shiva temples, five Vishnu temples, Buddhist and Jain monasteries, and a 7th-century market with a bath house. Xuanzang wrote of about 100 monasteries here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that central India had a great cosmopolitan city 1,400 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourteen centuries old and still standing, in brick.

spotlights.name: Rajiv Lochan Temple, Rajim
spotlights.spot_it: A walled courtyard of stone, with tall pillars carved with river goddesses and Vishnu's forms.
spotlights.story_md: At the Mahanadi confluence of Rajim stands a Vishnu temple whose core dates to the 7th or 8th century. Its pillars carry tall carved figures: river goddesses, a Durga, Vishnu's avatars and couples, crisp enough that you can see jewellery and hair. The temple is still in worship and is the anchor of the Rajim fair each winter. Pilgrims say a trip to Jagannath at Puri is not complete without Rajim, and many Chhattisgarhis visit both.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The oldest of the region's living Vishnu temples, still in daily use.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stone river goddesses guard the temple where three rivers meet.

spotlights.name: Ratanpur: Mahamaya temple and fort
spotlights.when: Kalachuri capital from about the 11th century
spotlights.spot_it: A temple with a domed hall beside tanks, and the ruined walls and gate of an old fort nearby.
spotlights.story_md: For centuries Chhattisgarh's capital was Ratanpur, seat of the Kalachuri (Haihaya) kings who ruled the plain from around 1000 CE until the Marathas arrived in the 1740s. A branch later moved to Raipur. The Mahamaya temple, dedicated to Durga as slayer of the buffalo demon, is counted by devotees among the Shakti Peethas and draws large crowds at Navratri. The ruined fort, temples and tanks around it show how big the town once was. Ratanpur's long Kalachuri rule is why many historians prefer to derive the state's name from Chedisgarh, the land of the Chedi (Kalachuri) kings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The political centre of the plains for most of the last thousand years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before Raipur, the capital was Ratanpur.

spotlights.name: Bhoramdeo Temple

where.label: Chaura village, 18 km from Kawardha, Kabirdham district

spotlights.spot_it: A stone Shiva temple at the foot of the Maikal hills, its walls wrapped in bands of dancers, gods and erotic couples.
spotlights.story_md: Bhoramdeo is called the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh, and the name tells you what to look for: tiers of carved figures, including couples in Kama Sutra poses, on the outer walls of a Shiva temple at the edge of the forest. It was finished around 1089 and is linked to the Phani Naga kings who ruled this corner under the Kalachuris. A kilometre away is the Madwa Mahal, a Shiva temple built in 1349 to mark a royal wedding, with 54 erotic images. Bhoramdeo itself is a local Gond name for Shiva, so the temple carries a tribal god's name on a classical building.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best-preserved medieval temple in the state, and a meeting of Gond and Hindu worship.
spotlights.memory_hook: Khajuraho's cousin, hiding in the Maikal forest.

sections.title: How it became a state
sections.intro_md:
The Marathas of Nagpur took the Kalachuri lands in the 1740s and 1750s, ruled through governors, and taxed hard. When the Nagpur kingdom passed to the British in 1854, Chhattisgarh became a division of the Central Provinces, run from Nagpur. Railways came in the 1880s and 1890s, and Raipur, Bilaspur and Rajnandgaon grew into market towns for rice and cotton.

Two revolts mark the colonial century. In 1857 Vir Narayan Singh, a landlord of Sonakhan, rose against the British and was hanged in Raipur. In 1910 the Adivasis of Bastar rose in the Bhumkal, the earthquake, against forest laws that took away their woods.

After independence the region joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956. People here felt they were a distant hinterland of Bhopal, with mines and dams that served others. A separate-state movement grew from the 1950s and finally won: the Madhya Pradesh Reorganisation Act created Chhattisgarh on 1 November 2000, with Ajit Jogi as its first Chief Minister.

spotlights.name: Vir Narayan Singh

where.label: Sonakhan, Baloda Bazar district; hanged at Jaistambh Chowk, Raipur

spotlights.spot_it: A memorial at Sonakhan and a white pillar at Raipur's busiest crossing, Jaistambh Chowk.
spotlights.story_md: Narayan Singh was the zamindar of Sonakhan, a forest estate. In the famine of 1856 he opened a merchant's grain store and gave the grain to starving villagers. The British arrested him for it. In 1857, as the rebellion spread, Indian soldiers helped him escape from Raipur jail; he went home, raised about 500 men and fought a British force. He was captured and hanged on 10 December 1857 at the spot now called Jaistambh Chowk in Raipur. Chhattisgarh calls him its first martyr of 1857; the international cricket stadium in Raipur and a new memorial museum opened in November 2025 carry his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state's founding hero, and a story about food before politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: He broke into a grain store in a famine and died a rebel.

spotlights.name: The Bhumkal of 1910
spotlights.spot_it: Look for it in Bastar's statues of Gunda Dhur and in place names; no photograph of the leader exists.
spotlights.story_md: In early 1910, messengers carried strange bundles from village to village across Bastar: red chillies, mango twigs, lumps of earth, clay bows and arrows. They were a call to rise. The Bhumkal (earthquake) was an Adivasi revolt against the princely state's officials and British forest policy, which had reserved forests and restricted the people who lived in them. Led by Gunda Dhur of Nethanar, the rebels attacked markets, police posts and officials' houses and surrounded Jagdalpur. British troops crushed it within months, helped by an informer. Gunda Dhur was never caught. In 2026 the government named its new service centres in Bastar after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first great forest-rights revolt in central India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chillies and mango twigs: the invitation to an uprising.

spotlights.name: Jagdalpur palace and the Bastar kings
spotlights.spot_it: A white palace in Jagdalpur, and a turbaned descendant who still leads the Dussehra rites.
spotlights.story_md: The Bastar rulers claimed descent from the Kakatiyas of Warangal, through Annam Dev, said to be a brother of King Prataparudra, who came north after the fall of Warangal in the 1320s. Historians call that link tenuous, but the claim shaped the court. In 1901 Bastar state covered about 33,831 km², larger than Belgium, and had about 300,000 people. It joined India on 1 January 1948. The last ruler, Pravir Chandra Bhanj Deo, was adored by many Adivasis and fought the government over land. On 25 March 1966 he was shot dead in a police action at his palace in Jagdalpur. His family still plays the king's role in Bastar Dussehra.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Explains why a tribal region still has a king in its festivals.
spotlights.memory_hook: A kingdom bigger than Belgium, with its king shot on his own steps.

sections.title: People and languages
sections.intro_md:
Chhattisgarh has two cultural halves that meet and mix. The plains are Chhattisgarhi-speaking farming country: Kurmi, Sahu (Teli), Yadav (Raut), Satnami and other castes, with Hindi in schools and offices. The hills and forests, above all Bastar in the south and Surguja and Jashpur in the north, are Adivasi country.

Census 2011 counted 7.8 million Scheduled Tribe people, 30.6 per cent of the state, one of the highest shares among large states. The biggest group is the Gond, with many branches: the Muria and the Maria (Madia) of Bastar, the Dorla near the Godavari. Others include the Halba, Bhatra, Oraon (Kurukh), Kanwar, Baiga and the Pahadi Korwa. The Baiga, Pahadi Korwa, Abujhmaria and Birhor are classed as particularly vulnerable groups.

Language follows the same map. Chhattisgarhi, an Eastern Hindi language with about 16 million speakers in 2011, has been co-official since 2007. Bastar runs on Halbi, a trade language used between tribes, and on Gondi, a Dravidian language. Surguja has its own dialect, Surgujia.

spotlights.name: The Gond

where.label: Across the state, largest in Bastar and the north

spotlights.when: Largest Adivasi people of central India
spotlights.spot_it: Clan shrines with flags and spears at the village edge, and offerings to Persa Pen, the clan god.
spotlights.story_md: The Gond are the largest Adivasi people of central India, spread across Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana and Odisha. Their language, Gondi, is Dravidian, related to Telugu rather than Hindi. Gond kingdoms once ruled much of the region, and Gondwana, the name geologists gave to the ancient southern supercontinent, comes from this land. Gond religion centres on clan gods, Persa Pen among them, and ancestors who must be fed. Many villages put up memorial stones for the dead. In Bastar, Gond subgroups such as the Muria and Maria keep their own dances, dormitories and councils.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The people whose land, language and gods underlie much of the state.
spotlights.memory_hook: A whole supercontinent is named after Gond country.

spotlights.name: Baiga and their godna tattoos

where.label: Kawardha, Mungeli and Bilaspur districts, Maikal hills

spotlights.spot_it: Women with dense blue-black lines and dots across forehead, arms, back and legs.
spotlights.story_md: The Baiga live in the Maikal hills on both sides of the Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh border. They were once shifting cultivators and are still known as healers with deep knowledge of forest plants. Baiga women are tattooed (godna) from girlhood in set patterns: different designs at different ages, forehead first, legs and back later. A common saying is that the tattoo is the only ornament you take with you when you die. The tattoos are done by women of another community, with needles and lampblack. Younger Baiga women are taking fewer of them, so the full-body godna is becoming a mark of older generations.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One of the clearest examples of the body as a record of identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only jewellery you take to the grave.

spotlights.name: The ghotul of the Muria

where.label: Muria villages around Narayanpur and Kondagaon, Bastar

spotlights.when: Described by Verrier Elwin in the 1940s
spotlights.spot_it: A larger hut at the village edge with carved wooden posts, where young unmarried people gather in the evening.
spotlights.story_md: The ghotul is a youth house. In many Muria villages, unmarried boys (chelik) and girls (motiari) spend their evenings there under elders' rules, learning songs, dances, work, discipline and service to the village. Gond legend says the god Lingo built the first one. The anthropologist Verrier Elwin called it a children's republic and wrote a famous, much-debated book about it in the 1940s. Outsiders later sensationalised it as a place of free love, which Muria people resent. Fewer villages keep a ghotul today, but many are being rebuilt as community halls.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A rare institution where the young run their own society.
spotlights.memory_hook: A village with a parliament for its teenagers.

sections.title: Faith: goddesses, gurus and the name of Ram
sections.intro_md:
Most people in Chhattisgarh are Hindu, and Hinduism here has strong local shapes. In Bastar the great goddess is Danteshwari, the family deity of the old kings, and village goddesses (mata, mavli) travel to festivals in palanquins. On the plains, Ram is everywhere: the state calls itself his maternal home, and Ram Navami and Ramayana recitations fill the calendar.

Two reform movements born here challenged caste. In the early 19th century Guru Ghasidas founded the **Satnami** path, rejecting idols and caste. In the 1890s the **Ramnami Samaj** turned the name of Ram into a tattoo of defiance. The Kabir Panth, followers of the poet Kabir, has a major seat at Damakheda.

Christians, about 2 per cent in 2011, are concentrated in Jashpur and Surguja. Conversion, and the backlash to it, has become a sharp political issue in parts of Bastar.

spotlights.name: Danteshwari temple, Dantewada

where.label: Dantewada, at the meeting of the Shankhini and Dankini rivers

spotlights.spot_it: A stone temple at a river confluence with a black stone image of the goddess, and a Garuda pillar at the gate.
spotlights.story_md: Dantewada takes its name from the goddess Danteshwari, from danta, tooth: tradition says a tooth of Sati fell here, which makes it one of the Shakti Peethas. The temple sits where two rivers meet and was built around the 14th century. Danteshwari was the family goddess of the Bastar kings, and she sits at the centre of Bastar Dussehra: her umbrella and palanquin travel to Jagdalpur, where a second Danteshwari temple, with a white image, hosts the festival. During Navratri thousands of oil lamps (jyoti kalash) are lit at Dantewada.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The spiritual centre of Bastar.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town named after a goddess's tooth.

spotlights.name: Guru Ghasidas and Giroudpuri
spotlights.spot_it: A white pillar flying a white flag, the jaitkham, in Satnami villages; at Giroudpuri, a white tower taller than the Qutub Minar.
spotlights.story_md: Ghasidas was born into a Dalit family at Giroudpuri in 1756. He taught Satnam, the true name: one formless God, no idols, no meat, no alcohol, no caste. Followers dropped caste names and took the name Satnami. Their symbol is the jaitkham, a white-painted pole with a white flag, which still stands in Satnami villages across the plains. Giroudpuri, his birthplace by the Mahanadi, holds a huge fair each year, and its concrete jaitkham, opened in 2015, is about 77 m tall, higher than the Qutub Minar. His birthday, 18 December, is a state holiday, and Bilaspur's central university bears his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Dalit reform movement that reshaped a large part of the state's society and politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: A white flag on a white pole: the sign of Satnam.

spotlights.name: The Ramnami Samaj

where.label: Villages along the Mahanadi, Janjgir-Champa, Raigarh and Baloda Bazar

spotlights.spot_it: Every visible inch of skin tattooed with राम, white shawls printed with the name, and crowns of peacock feathers.
spotlights.story_md: In the 1890s a Dalit man named Parasuram was refused entry to a temple. His answer was to tattoo the name Ram on his forehead: if he could not go to God, he would carry God on his body. The Ramnami Samaj grew from that act. Members tattoo Ram on their bodies, the most devoted on every part of the body; they wear shawls printed with the name, avoid alcohol, and chant all day. Upper-caste Hindus took them to court over their use of Ram's name; the Ramnamis won in 1910. They have no temple and no idol. Their great annual gathering is the three-day Bade Bhajan Mela. Few young members now take full tattoos, for fear of discrimination at work.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A protest against caste written in ink on human skin.
spotlights.memory_hook: Locked out of the temple, he wrote God on his face.

spotlights.name: Kaushalya Mata temple, Chandkhuri
spotlights.when: Old shrine; rebuilt and reopened about 2021
spotlights.spot_it: A small temple on an island in a lake, with a giant standing Ram statue outside.
spotlights.story_md: Chhattisgarh calls itself Rama's maternal home, because local belief makes Chandkhuri, near Raipur, the parental village of Queen Kaushalya, Rama's mother. Her temple sits in a lake and is said to be one of very few anywhere dedicated to her. The state rebuilt the complex as the first stop on its Ram Van Gaman Path, a tourism circuit tracing Rama's supposed exile route through Dandakaranya, and added a tall statue of Rama. People here often speak of Rama as their bhanja, their sister's son, and some families touch the feet of a sister's son for that reason.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A key to why Ram is so central to the state's public identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Chhattisgarh, Ram is the nephew.

sections.title: Song, dance and theatre
sections.intro_md:
Chhattisgarh's performing arts are mostly village arts, tied to a community and a season. The plains have **Pandavani**, the Mahabharata sung by one performer with a tambura; **Panthi**, the Satnamis' devotional dance; **Raut Nacha**, the cowherds' stick dance after Diwali; **Sua**, women dancing around a clay parrot; and **Karma**, danced around a branch of the karam tree. Bastar has the **Gaur** dance of the Bison-horn Maria and many drum dances.

The plains also had **Nacha**, a rough, comic folk theatre of all-night shows with men in women's roles. In the 1970s Habib Tanvir took Nacha actors from Chhattisgarh villages to Delhi and then to Edinburgh, and they won.

Watch the clips: Pandavani is easier to understand when you see a single woman turn a tambura into a mace, a bow and a chariot in under a minute.

rows.kapalik: Memory and oral tradition, freely improvised
rows.vedamati: A fixed verse text of the Mahabharata

rows.kapalik: Standing, moving, acting out the fight

spotlights.name: Pandavani

where.label: Villages of the Chhattisgarh plain, especially Durg and Bhilai

spotlights.when: Old ballad form; women from the late 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: One singer with a tambura hung with bells, a small band behind on harmonium and dholak, and a chorus that answers.
spotlights.story_md: Pandavani means the story of the Pandavas. A single performer sings and acts episodes of the Mahabharata, usually with Bhima as the hero, while a ragi, a companion singer, asks questions and adds jokes and a few musicians keep time. The tambura, sometimes tied with bells and peacock feathers, is the only prop: it becomes Bhima's mace, Arjuna's bow, a chariot, Draupadi's loose hair. There are two schools. Vedamati follows a written verse text; Kapalik is improvised from memory. For generations the performers were men. Teejan Bai changed that, and today women like Usha Barle and Ritu Verma lead troupes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Chhattisgarh's most famous art form, and the epic as one person's theatre.
spotlights.memory_hook: One woman, one tambura, eighteen books of war.

spotlights.name: Teejan Bai

where.label: Ganiyari village, near Bhilai, Durg district

spotlights.spot_it: A big voice, a tambura raised like a mace, and a face that turns from Bhima to Draupadi in a second.
spotlights.story_md: Teejan Bai was born in 1956 into the Pardhi tribe at Ganiyari, near Bhilai. She learned Pandavani from her grandfather, against her family's wishes. At 13 she sang in public, standing, in the Kapalik style, when women were expected to sit. She paid for it: she was cast out and her first marriage broke. Habib Tanvir saw her, took her to Delhi and to Indira Gandhi, and she went on to perform across Europe and Asia. She won the Padma Shri (1988), Padma Bhushan (2003), Fukuoka Prize (2018) and Padma Vibhushan (2019). She died at AIIMS Raipur on 5 July 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made a men's art into a woman's, and Chhattisgarh's best-known voice abroad.
spotlights.memory_hook: She stood up to sing, and never sat down again.

spotlights.name: Panthi

where.label: Satnami villages of the plains; Giroudpuri

spotlights.when: Danced especially around 18 December, Guru Ghasidas Jayanti
spotlights.spot_it: Men in white with a mandar drum and cymbals, around a jaitkham, building speed to a whirl and finishing in human pyramids.
spotlights.story_md: Panthi is the dance of the Satnami community, sung in praise of Guru Ghasidas. A group of men in white vests and dhotis, often with a jaitkham at the centre, start slowly with a lead singer and a mandar drum and jhanjh cymbals. The tempo rises and rises until the dancers spin, kneel, leap and finish by climbing on each other's shoulders into pyramids. The songs carry the guru's teachings: truth, equality, no idols. Devdas Banjare made it famous on national and foreign stages from the 1970s. It is now standard at state functions, but its meaning remains the Satnami message.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dance that carries a social reform movement's message.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slow hymn, fast whirl, human pyramid.

spotlights.name: Raut Nacha

where.label: Plains villages; big gathering in Bilaspur

spotlights.when: From Dev Uthani Ekadashi, after Diwali
spotlights.spot_it: Men in bright frilled costumes, peacock feathers and cowries, beating sticks and small shields and shouting rhyming couplets.
spotlights.story_md: The Raut, or Yadav, are the cowherds of the plains, and Raut Nacha is their dance for Krishna, the god who herded cows. It begins on Dev Uthani Ekadashi, when the gods are said to wake from their monsoon sleep, a few days after Diwali, and runs through the market fairs that follow. Dancers wear colourful frocks, turbans with feathers, and strings of cowries; they clash sticks like a mock battle and, between rounds, a dancer shouts a doha, a rhyming couplet, often witty or teasing, while the gadwa band plays. Bilaspur holds a large Raut Nacha festival each November.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The dance that marks the end of the farming year in the plains.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sticks clash, a couplet is shouted, the cows are blessed.

spotlights.name: Sua nacha, the parrot dance
spotlights.spot_it: Women in a circle, clapping in rhythm around a basket holding a clay parrot.
spotlights.story_md: Sua means parrot. In the weeks around Diwali, groups of women and girls go from house to house, set a basket with a clay or wooden parrot in the middle, and dance around it, clapping and singing. There are no drums: the claps are the rhythm. The songs are addressed to the parrot, the messenger bird of Indian love poetry, and many are about separation, a wife's longing, or the hardship of a woman's life. Households give rice or money. It is one of the few dances in the region that is entirely women's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A women's art of song and clapping, still alive in villages.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tell the parrot what you cannot tell your husband.

spotlights.name: Gaur dance of the Bison-horn Maria

where.label: Abujhmarh and around Narayanpur and Dantewada

spotlights.spot_it: Men in tall headdresses of bison horns, cowries and feathers, drumming as they dance; women in a line with iron staffs that jingle.
spotlights.story_md: The Maria of southern Bastar dance the gaur at weddings and festivals. The men wear headdresses topped with bison (gaur) horns, or carved wooden horns, decorated with cowrie shells, peacock and other feathers and strands of beads hanging over the face, and they carry big drums slung at the waist. They mimic the charge and sparring of bison. Women dance in a line, wearing brass and bead ornaments and beating iron staffs hung with rings. British administrators named the people the Bison-horn Maria after the headdress.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most photographed image of Bastar's dance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dancer with bison horns and a drum: the gaur charges.

spotlights.name: Habib Tanvir and Nacha theatre
spotlights.spot_it: Folk actors from Chhattisgarh speaking their own dialect on a bare stage, with songs and a chorus.
spotlights.story_md: Habib Tanvir was born in Raipur in 1923, trained in London and Bristol, and came home convinced that India's theatre should start from its villages. In 1959 he founded Naya Theatre and recruited Nacha performers, folk actors from Chhattisgarh villages, who acted in their own Chhattisgarhi. Their greatest hit was Charandas Chor (1975), the story of a thief who has vowed never to lie and dies for it. In 1982 it won a Fringe First at the Edinburgh festival. Tanvir also gave Teejan Bai her first national stage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He proved that village actors could carry world theatre.
spotlights.memory_hook: A thief who never lies, played by villagers, wins in Edinburgh.

sections.title: Crafts: metal, iron, silk and mud walls
sections.intro_md:
Bastar is one of India's great craft districts, and most of it is made by communities whose craft was once a service to the village: the Ghadwa cast brass for ritual and trade, the Lohar forged iron tools, the potters made horses and elephants for the gods. Kondagaon, on the road from Raipur to Jagdalpur, is now the busiest workshop town.

The plains have silk. Around Champa and Janjgir, weavers make **kosa**, the state's tussar silk, from cocoons of wild silkworms gathered in the forest. In Surguja, Rajwar women model relief patterns in mud on house walls.

Several of these crafts have Geographical Indication tags: Bastar Dhokra was registered in 2008, and Champa silk sarees are also listed. Watch for fakes: a lot of machine-cast brass in city shops is sold as Bastar dhokra.

spotlights.name: Bastar dhokra (bell metal)
spotlights.spot_it: Brass figures whose whole surface is covered in fine raised lines and spirals, as if wrapped in thread.
spotlights.story_md: Dhokra is lost-wax casting, one of the oldest metal techniques in the world. In Bastar the Ghadwa community make a clay core, then cover it with threads of beeswax and resin, winding and coiling them into eyes, jewellery, tails and patterns. That is why Bastar pieces look as if they are made of string. Clay goes over the wax, the mould is baked, the wax runs out, and molten brass is poured into the space it left. Each mould is broken to free the piece, so no two are the same. Subjects are deities, elephants, horses, lamps, tribal musicians and hunters. Jaidev Baghel of Kondagaon became its best-known master.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bastar's signature craft, sold in every Indian craft shop.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every line on a Bastar horse was once a thread of wax.

spotlights.name: Bastar wrought iron
spotlights.when: Old village smithing; now a studio craft
spotlights.spot_it: Tall, thin, black iron figures and lamps, hammered from a single bar, with no welding.
spotlights.story_md: The Lohar (blacksmith) families of Bastar once made ploughshares, axes and arrowheads for their villages, and votive figures for the gods. Today the same skills produce tall, spindly figures of hunters, musicians, deer and many-armed lamps. The rule of the craft is that the pieces are shaped by heating and hammering from scrap iron, and joined by hammering, not by welding. Up close you can see hammer marks and twisted rods. Much of the scrap now comes from old vehicles and railway iron.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tool-making tradition turned into sculpture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Scrap iron, fire and a hammer: no welding allowed.

spotlights.name: Kosa silk
spotlights.when: Old weaving centre; Champa silk listed as a GI
spotlights.spot_it: A dull gold, slightly rough silk with a natural sheen, often woven with bold borders.
spotlights.story_md: Kosa is Chhattisgarh's name for tussar silk. It is made by wild silkworms, Antheraea species, that feed on forest trees such as arjun, saja and sal rather than on mulberry. Forest families collect or rear the cocoons; weaver families in Champa and Janjgir reel and weave them into sarees and fabric. The natural colour is a deep honey gold; mulberry silk is whiter and smoother. Kosa is coarser and has shorter fibres, so it feels drier and more textured, and it takes dyes well. Raigarh and Champa sarees are the best known.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Connects the forest economy to the weaver's loom.
spotlights.memory_hook: Silk grown on forest trees, the colour of honey.

spotlights.name: Surguja mud-relief walls
spotlights.spot_it: Raised mud reliefs of birds, trees, lattices and figures on whitewashed village walls.
spotlights.story_md: In Surguja, women of the Rajwar and other communities decorate their houses with raised reliefs made from mud, cow dung and husk, modelled by hand on the walls and then whitewashed or painted. The designs include birds, animals, trees, women carrying pots, and lattice windows that are part decoration, part ventilation. Sona Bai Rajwar of Puhputra village became famous for turning her whole house into a sculpted world and received national recognition. The walls are renewed before festivals, so the art is always being remade.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A women's architecture of mud, living and changing every year.
spotlights.memory_hook: A house that is also a sculpture.

spotlights.name: Memorial stones of Bastar
spotlights.spot_it: Upright slabs of stone or carved wooden pillars by the roadside, sometimes painted with scenes of the dead person's life.
spotlights.story_md: Drive through Bastar and you pass groups of standing stones at village edges. Among the Gond, Maria and Muria, these are memorials to the dead. Families raise a stone slab, sometimes very large, and hold a feast; some groups carve or paint wooden pillars showing the dead person's life: a cow, a bicycle, a motorbike, a bus, a policeman, a gun. Modern memorials sometimes use concrete and paint. The stones mark a belief that the dead stay close to the village and must be honoured.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A record of lives that no archive holds.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bicycle painted on a grave post: the dead man's pride.

sections.title: Food: rice, ants and mahua
sections.intro_md:
Chhattisgarhi food is rice food, eaten in every form: soaked overnight, steamed as dumplings, ground into batter for pancakes, puffed and sweetened. Pulses, leafy greens (bhaji, of which villages name dozens), curd and simple chutneys complete the plate. It is plain, frugal and filling food made for hard field work, and outside the state it is almost unknown.

Bastar adds the forest: mushrooms after the first rain, bamboo shoots, tamarind, red-ant chutney, mahua flowers, the sap of the sulfi palm, and a sour rice drink called landa.

The dishes to know: **chila** (a rice-flour pancake), **fara** (steamed rice dumplings), **muthia**, **angakar roti** (a thick rice bread baked on leaves), **dubki kadhi** (dumplings in a yogurt curry), **bore basi** (rice soaked overnight), **tikhur** (a starch from a forest root, cooked into a cooling sweet), and **chapda** chutney.

spotlights.name: Chila
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, lacy pancake of rice-flour batter, soft rather than crisp, served with tomato or green chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Chila is the dosa of Chhattisgarh, but simpler: rice flour, water, salt, sometimes green chilli and onion, poured onto a hot pan, often an earthenware one, and cooked with very little oil. There is no fermentation and no lentil. Eaten hot with a sharp tomato chutney, it is breakfast in countless homes. A cousin, angakar roti, is a thick round of rice dough baked between leaves over embers. Fara are the leftovers turned into a second dish: rice dough rolled into thin fingers, steamed, and then tossed with mustard seeds and chillies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The simplest way into the cuisine, and easy to cook at home.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice, water, salt, a hot pan: chila.

spotlights.name: Chapda, red-ant chutney
spotlights.when: Made through the year; peak in the hot months
spotlights.spot_it: A coarse red-brown paste of crushed ants and their white eggs, ground with chilli, salt and garlic, sold in leaf cups at markets.
spotlights.story_md: In Bastar's markets women sell nests of red weaver ants (Oecophylla smaragdina), which build balls of leaves stitched together with silk from their larvae. The ants and their eggs are shaken out, crushed on a stone with chilli, salt, garlic and sometimes ginger, and eaten as chapda chutney. It tastes sharply sour, because the ants contain formic acid. People eat it against fever and colds and as a relish with rice. The chef Gordon Ramsay tasted it in Bastar while filming in 2010, which made it briefly famous. Odisha's Similipal version received a GI tag in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Forest protein and sourness in one spoon, and Bastar's most talked-about food.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chutney that bites back.

spotlights.name: Mahua

where.label: Forests across the state, especially Bastar and Surguja

spotlights.when: Flowers fall in March and April
spotlights.spot_it: Fleshy cream-coloured flowers carpeting the ground under a broad tree before dawn, then drying in the sun on mats.
spotlights.story_md: The mahua tree (Madhuca longifolia) drops its flowers at night in spring, and whole families go out before dawn to collect them. The flowers are thick and sugary. Dried, they are eaten, cooked into laddoos and sold to traders; fermented and distilled, they become mahua, the clear spirit of central India's forest villages, offered to gods and ancestors and drunk at festivals. The seeds give an oil used for cooking and soap. For many Adivasi households mahua flowers and sal seeds are a major source of cash in a lean season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tree that feeds, pays and intoxicates the forest villages.
spotlights.memory_hook: The tree that rains sugar at night.

spotlights.name: Bore basi
spotlights.when: Summer staple; Bore Basi Tihar on 1 May
spotlights.spot_it: A bowl of cooked rice sitting in its own water, eaten cold with salt, onion, green chilli and a fried vegetable or chutney.
spotlights.story_md: Bore basi is rice cooked the night before and left to soak in water, often with some of its starchy cooking water, until morning. It ferments a little, turns faintly sour and becomes cooling, which is why labourers and farmers eat it before going out in the summer heat. Bore is the fresh version, basi the overnight one. Studies have found more of some minerals in it than in plain cooked rice. Odisha's pakhala is the same idea. In 2022 the state government began marking 1 May, Labour Day, as Bore Basi Tihar, with the Chief Minister eating it in public.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The worker's breakfast, made into a state symbol.
spotlights.memory_hook: Yesterday's rice, today's lunch, tomorrow's holiday.

spotlights.name: The rice bowl and its 20,000 rices
spotlights.spot_it: Small-plot trials of dozens of rice varieties, each a different height and colour, at the agricultural university in Raipur.
spotlights.story_md: Chhattisgarh is called the rice bowl of India. The plain grows paddy as far as you can see, and the state now buys it from farmers at ₹3,100 a quintal, far above the national minimum price. But the bigger treasure is diversity. In the 1970s the rice scientist R. H. Richharia led the collection of traditional varieties from the region's farmers: some 19,000 from Chhattisgarh alone. Around 20,000 rice accessions are now kept at Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya in Raipur, most from this region. Two local rices have GI tags: aromatic Jeeraphool from Surguja (2019) and Nagri Dubraj from Dhamtari (2023).
spotlights.why_it_matters: A living library of rice that India may need as the climate changes.
spotlights.memory_hook: One state, twenty thousand rices.

sections.title: Festivals: a 75-day Dussehra and a year of farm feasts
sections.intro_md:
The festival calendar follows the paddy. **Hareli**, in the month of Shravan (July or August), opens the farming year: tools are washed and worshipped, neem twigs hung at doorways, and children walk on bamboo stilts called gedi. **Pola**, a month later, honours the bullocks. **Teeja** brings married women home to their parents. Diwali is followed by Govardhan puja, the **Raut Nacha** and the **Sua** dance. Then come the winter **madai** fairs and the great river fair at **Rajim**.

Bastar has its own cycle, built around village gods who travel. Its centrepiece, **Bastar Dussehra**, runs for about 75 days and ends, in 2026, this very week. In spring, Dantewada holds the Phagun madai, and every village has its own fair when the local goddess receives visiting gods.

For the Satnamis, 18 December (Guru Ghasidas Jayanti) and the Giroudpuri fair are the high points of the year.

spotlights.name: Bastar Dussehra
spotlights.when: About 75 days, from Hariyali Amavasya; in 2026 from 12 August to late October
spotlights.spot_it: A two-storey wooden chariot pulled by hundreds of villagers with ropes through Jagdalpur, the goddess Danteshwari's umbrella on top. No Ravana anywhere.
spotlights.story_md: Bastar Dussehra has nothing to do with Rama's victory. It honours Danteshwari and hundreds of village deities, and it lasts about 75 days. It opens with Pat Jatra, the worship of a sal log for the chariot. A girl of the Mirgan community, possessed by the goddess Kachhin Devi, gives permission from a swing. A man sits in a pit in meditation for nine days (Jogi Bithai). Villagers from set communities build the chariot by hand and pull it around the town. On Bahar Raini night, men from nearby villages steal the chariot and hide it at Kumhdakot, a few kilometres away; the king must go and bring it back after offering new rice to the goddess. The festival ends with the Muria Darbar, where village headmen once put their complaints to the king. Tradition dates it to King Purushottam Dev around 1408.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The longest Dussehra in India and a living map of Bastar's villages and gods.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Dussehra where the chariot is stolen and Ravana never shows up.

spotlights.name: Hareli
spotlights.when: Shravan Amavasya (July or August); a state holiday
spotlights.spot_it: Ploughs, hoes and sickles washed and laid out with offerings; neem twigs tucked above doors; children tottering on tall bamboo stilts.
spotlights.story_md: Hareli comes from hariyali, greenness: it falls on the new moon of Shravan, when the paddy has been sown and the fields are green. Farmers wash their ploughs and tools and worship them along with the cattle; the herdsman hangs neem or bhelwa twigs on every door to keep away disease and evil. Children make gedi, bamboo stilts, and walk on them through the muddy lanes until the festival of Pola, when the stilts are put away. Chhattisgarhi dishes like chila and gulgula (sweet fritters) are cooked. The state made Hareli a public holiday in 2019 and holds gedi races and traditional games.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first festival of the farming year, and the most Chhattisgarhi of all.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stilts out at Hareli, stilts away at Pola.

spotlights.name: Rajim fair (Punni Mela)
spotlights.when: Magh Purnima to Mahashivratri (February to March)
spotlights.spot_it: Tents, stalls and sadhus spread over the dry Mahanadi riverbed between the Rajiv Lochan and Kuleshwar temples.
spotlights.story_md: For about two weeks each year, the dry bed of the Mahanadi at Rajim turns into a town. Pilgrims bathe at the meeting of the Mahanadi, Pairi and Sondur, worship at the Rajiv Lochan temple and at the Kuleshwar Mahadev temple on an island in the river, and shop at stalls of bangles, utensils and sweets. The state promoted it for some years as the Rajim Kumbh, inviting sadhus from the great Kumbh fairs, and later returned to its older local name, Punni Mela. Whatever it is called, it is the biggest fair of the Chhattisgarh plain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The plains' great river pilgrimage.
spotlights.memory_hook: A town that appears on the riverbed every February.

sections.title: How people live
sections.intro_md:
Most people in Chhattisgarh live in villages: about 77 per cent at the 2011 census, one of the most rural populations among Indian states. Life follows paddy and forest. In the plains, a family's year is sowing in June and July, transplanting, weeding, harvest in November, then selling paddy to the government at a procurement centre between November and January. Many then migrate for months to brick kilns and building sites in other states.

In the forest, the calendar is set by what the trees give: mahua in March and April, tendu leaves (for bidis) in May, sal seeds in June, mushrooms and bamboo shoots in the rains. These are collected and sold at the weekly **haat**, the market that is also post office, bank, courtroom and dating scene.

The state's own slogan is *Chhattisgarhiya sabse badhiya*: Chhattisgarhis are the best. It is half joke, half answer to the stereotype of a poor, simple people. The 2011 sex ratio of 991 women per 1,000 men was among the best of the larger states. But NITI Aayog's multidimensional poverty index put about 16 per cent of people in poverty in 2019 to 2021, down from about 30 per cent five years earlier, but still above the national figure of about 15 per cent.

spotlights.name: The weekly haat

where.label: Weekly markets across Bastar, such as Farasgaon and Narayanpur

spotlights.when: Once a week in each market village
spotlights.spot_it: A field filled once a week: women with baskets of tamarind and mahua, a barber under a tree, a cockfight ring, stalls of beads and aluminium pots.
spotlights.story_md: In Bastar the haat is how the week is counted. People walk in from villages up to a day away carrying forest produce: tamarind, mahua flowers, sal seeds, honey, mushrooms, red-ant nests, broomgrass. Traders buy, and the sellers buy salt, oil, cloth, beads and tools. Barbers, tailors and bicycle repairers set up under trees, and there is usually a cockfight ring in the corner. Families meet relatives from other villages, marriages are arranged, disputes are settled, and young people meet. Prices are often set by measure, a bowl of tamarind for a bowl of salt, rather than by weight.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The single best window into Bastar's economy and social life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bastar's week has one day that matters: market day.

sections.title: How it earns: coal, iron, steel and rice
sections.intro_md:
Chhattisgarh is one of the minerals capitals of India. It holds about 18 per cent of the country's coal reserves and in recent years produced around a fifth of its coal. Its iron ore from Bailadila is among the richest in the world. It is the only state producing tin concentrate, and it mines bauxite and limestone for aluminium and cement. On that base sit Bhilai's steel plant, Korba's power stations and BALCO's aluminium smelter, plus dozens of sponge iron plants around Raipur and Raigarh.

The state economy was about ₹5.09 lakh crore (about US$53 billion) in 2023 to 24. Agriculture still employs most workers: paddy on the plains, and minor forest produce in the forest belt. In the 2024 to 25 season the state bought a record 149.25 lakh tonnes of paddy from about 25.5 lakh farmers.

The tension at the heart of the economy is simple to state: the minerals lie under the forests, and the forests are where Adivasis live.

spotlights.name: Bhilai Steel Plant
spotlights.when: Founded 1955 with Soviet help; production from 1959
spotlights.spot_it: Blast furnaces and a company town of tree-lined sectors; India's rails come out of here.
spotlights.story_md: In 1955 India and the Soviet Union agreed to build a steel plant in a village called Bhilai. Production began in 1959, and a planned township grew around it, with schools so good that Bhilai became known for producing engineers and doctors. The plant of the Steel Authority of India is India's main maker of rails and the sole supplier of 260-metre long rails, the longest made in the country. It has won the Prime Minister's Trophy for the best integrated steel plant eleven times. At its peak it employed nearly 60,000 people. Bhilai also gave the state a cosmopolitan population from every part of India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The Nehru-era factory that made the region industrial.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every long rail on Indian Railways starts at Bhilai.

spotlights.name: Gevra and Korba: the coal and power hub
spotlights.when: Gevra opened 1981; 59 million tonnes in 2023 to 24
spotlights.spot_it: A pit kilometres long, dumpers bigger than houses, and the cooling towers of Korba on the horizon.
spotlights.story_md: Korba is the power capital of the state, ringed by coal mines and power stations of NTPC and the state utility, plus BALCO's aluminium smelter. Its largest mine is Gevra, an open-cast pit run by South Eastern Coalfields that began in 1981. In 2023 to 24 it produced about 59 million tonnes of coal, and the Coal Ministry, citing a WorldAtlas list in 2024, called it the second-largest coal mine in the world, with Kusmunda nearby fourth. Its capacity is being expanded to 70 million tonnes a year. Villages around it have been moved, and the dust is a constant complaint.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Where much of India's electricity begins.
spotlights.memory_hook: Asia's biggest hole in the ground.

spotlights.name: Bailadila iron ore range
spotlights.spot_it: A long forested ridge shaped like a bull's hump, with red terraced mine benches cut into its top.
spotlights.story_md: Bailadila means the bull's hump, after the shape of the ridge. Its iron ore is famously rich, more than 60 per cent iron, and the state-owned NMDC has mined it since the 1960s. A railway was built across the Eastern Ghats from Kirandul to Kottavalasa near Visakhapatnam to carry ore to the port for export, much of it to Japan in the early decades. Today ore also goes to the new NMDC steel plant at Nagarnar near Jagdalpur. In 2019 Adivasis blockaded a planned mine on Nandraj hill, which they regard as sacred, and the project was paused.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The ore that pulled a railway through the forest.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bull's hump made of iron.

spotlights.name: Hasdeo Arand
spotlights.spot_it: Unbroken sal forest over rolling hills, with elephant trails, villages, and the edge of an open-cast coal mine eating into it.
spotlights.story_md: Hasdeo Arand is about 170,000 hectares of forest in the north, called the largest unfragmented forest in central India. Underneath lie about 5 billion tonnes of coal in 23 blocks. The Parsa East and Kete Basan block was allotted to Rajasthan's state power utility with Adani as mine operator, and tree felling for its expansions has repeatedly met protests by Gond villagers who say their gram sabha consent was faked. In July 2022 the assembly unanimously resolved against new mining in Hasdeo. Felling resumed in December 2023 and August 2024. In 2024 activist Alok Shukla won the Goldman Environmental Prize for the campaign. In 2025 a further forest diversion for the Kete Extension block was recommended, and the fight goes on.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clearest test of coal versus forest in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five billion tonnes of coal under India's most argued-over forest.

sections.title: The long war in Bastar
sections.intro_md:
From the 1980s, Maoist guerrillas moving north from Andhra Pradesh made the forests of Bastar, which they called Dandakaranya, their main base. They ran parallel governments in villages, taxed contractors, and fought the state. Bastar's poverty, its absent government and its grievances over land and forest gave them a foothold.

The war was brutal on all sides. In 2005 the state backed **Salwa Judum**, a militia of armed villagers; tens of thousands were displaced into camps, and in 2011 the Supreme Court declared the arming of civilians as special police officers unconstitutional. In April 2010 Maoists killed 76 security personnel at Tadmetla in Sukma. In May 2013, at Jhiram Ghati, they ambushed a Congress convoy and killed most of the state's Congress leadership, including Mahendra Karma, the Salwa Judum's founder. Adivasi villagers were caught between both sides, and killed by both.

From 2024 the government launched an offensive with a deadline of 31 March 2026. Hundreds of Maoists were killed and thousands surrendered.

spotlights.name: Abujhmarh, the unknown hills
spotlights.when: Never fully surveyed until the 2010s and 2020s
spotlights.spot_it: Forested hills with no roads, home of the Abujhmaria; until recently, the Maoists' headquarters.
spotlights.story_md: Abujh means unknowable. Abujhmarh is about 4,000 km² of forested hills where Narayanpur, Bijapur and Dantewada districts meet, home to the Abujhmaria, a particularly vulnerable tribal group. It was so remote that the British never surveyed its land, and for decades outsiders needed permission to enter. That isolation made it the heart of the Maoist movement. In May 2025 security forces killed CPI (Maoist) general secretary Nambala Keshava Rao, known as Basavaraju, and about 27 others in an encounter there, the first time in three decades the party's top leader was killed. By October 2025 the government declared Abujhmarh free of Maoists, and revenue surveys of its villages are now under way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The place where the insurgency lived longest, and where it ended.
spotlights.memory_hook: Abujh means unknowable: the last unmapped hills.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
**1 November 2025.** The state turned 25. Prime Minister Modi opened the new Vidhan Sabha in Nava Raipur, a memorial museum for Vir Narayan Singh and tribal freedom fighters, and projects worth over ₹14,260 crore.

**November 2025 to January 2026.** Paddy procurement ran at ₹3,100 a quintal, capped at 21 quintals an acre; by mid-December about 87 lakh tonnes had been bought.

**February 2026.** President Droupadi Murmu opened Bastar Pandum, a state festival of tribal arts in Jagdalpur, and spoke of an end to the atmosphere of fear in Bastar.

**30 March 2026.** Deputy Chief Minister and Home Minister Vijay Sharma declared the state 100 per cent free of armed Naxalism, a day ahead of the Centre's deadline.

**20 May 2026.** In Jagdalpur, Union Home Minister Amit Shah declared India Naxal-free and launched the Shaheed Veer Gunda Dhur Seva Dera scheme to turn about 70 security camps into service centres. Nearly 3,000 surrendered cadres were in rehabilitation. Critics continue to question the civilian cost of the campaign.

**5 July 2026.** Teejan Bai died in Raipur.

**August to October 2026.** Bastar Dussehra ran from 12 August, with the main chariot rites around 20 October.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md: Chhattisgarh is often described in a few lazy phrases: a Naxal state, a tribal state, a backward state. Each holds a piece of truth and hides more. Two-thirds of its people are not Adivasi; most of its land was never touched by the insurgency; and its sex ratio and food distribution have long been better than those of richer states. Some famous stories about its places are also stretched in the retelling. Here are the claims you will hear most often, tested against the evidence.

Scheduled Tribes were 30.6% in 2011. The plains are mostly non-tribal.
